lead: A valve timing diagram is a map of when the inlet and exhaust valves open and close, measured in crank angle degrees from top dead centre (TDC) and bottom dead centre (BDC). It exists because a four-stroke engine cannot breathe well if the valves open and close exactly at TDC and BDC. The same idea for a two-stroke engine is a port timing diagram. These diagrams guide cam design, tuning and fault finding on cars, motorcycles, gensets and pumps.
prereq: You need: four-stroke and two-stroke engines and working principle of SI and CI engines.

blocks.text: A four-stroke cycle takes 720° of crank rotation. In a valve timing diagram, 0° is TDC at the start of the intake stroke. The piston reaches BDC at 180°, TDC at 360°, BDC at 540° and TDC again at 720°. Angles are crank degrees (°CA), not cam degrees. The cam turns at half crank speed in a four-stroke engine.

The inlet valve does not open exactly at TDC. It opens before TDC by the inlet lead. It closes after BDC by the inlet lag. The exhaust valve opens before BDC by the exhaust lead and closes after TDC by the exhaust lag. Lead and lag use gas inertia: the exhaust needs a head start to blow down, and the incoming charge keeps moving after BDC.
Inlet open period = θ<sub>i,lead</sub> + 180° + θ<sub>i,lag</sub>; Exhaust open period = θ<sub>e,lead</sub> + 180° + θ<sub>e,lag</sub>; Valve overlap = θ<sub>i,lead</sub> + θ<sub>e,lag</sub>
blocks.where: θ<sub>i,lead</sub> is inlet lead before TDC; θ<sub>i,lag</sub> is inlet lag after BDC; θ<sub>e,lead</sub> is exhaust lead before BDC; θ<sub>e,lag</sub> is exhaust lag after TDC. All angles are in crank degrees. Overlap is the common open time around TDC.

blocks.text: Valve overlap is the short period when both valves are open. Near the end of exhaust, fresh charge can help push out burnt gas. Too much overlap at low speed can send fresh charge back into the inlet or let exhaust enter the cylinder. The diagram is used to check cam timing after assembly and to tune an engine.

sections.h3: SI and CI valve timing compared

blocks.text: Both SI and CI four-stroke engines use the same four events: inlet open, inlet close, exhaust open and exhaust close. The difference is in the size of the angles and the reason for them. An SI engine throttles the air-fuel mixture. At idle, the inlet pressure is low, so a large overlap can push exhaust gas back into the inlet. SI engines therefore use a small overlap at low speed. A CI engine has no throttle plate, so there is no air-fuel mixture to lose through overlap. But its high compression ratio leaves very little valve-to-piston clearance, and without a turbocharger the inlet pressure is not above the exhaust pressure. Naturally aspirated CI engines therefore use small overlap or none. Larger overlap is used in pressure-charged diesels, where boost pressure above exhaust pressure lets fresh air scavenge the clearance volume.

In an SI engine the inlet closes after BDC to use the ram effect of the moving mixture. In a CI engine the inlet also closes after BDC, but the trapped charge is only air; fuel is injected later. The exhaust valve opens before BDC in both engines. This blowdown, the early rush of burnt gas out of the cylinder, uses the remaining pressure to start the exhaust flow, so the piston does less pumping work on the upstroke.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this comparison a tutorial question. Answer it by naming the four events, giving the order, and explaining overlap. Do not write that CI engines have no valve overlap; they do, only the fuel injection event is different.

sections.h3: Port timing in a two-stroke engine

blocks.text: A two-stroke engine often uses ports cut in the cylinder wall instead of valves. The piston itself acts as the valve. A port timing diagram shows the crank angle at which each port is uncovered and covered. The exhaust port opens first, about 60° before BDC in many small engines. The transfer port opens a little later. On the upstroke the transfer port closes first and the exhaust port closes last. This order lets burnt gas leave before fresh charge enters and keeps the exhaust open while the charge is transferred.

In a simple piston-port engine the exhaust and transfer ports open and close at equal angles around BDC, so their timing is symmetric about BDC. The inlet port, if it is piston-controlled, is near TDC and is symmetric about TDC. Reed valves and rotary valves can make the inlet timing asymmetric. A two-stroke CI engine uses air scavenging and a fuel injector, but its exhaust and transfer port timing is read the same way.

A port timing diagram is not adjustable like a camshaft. The port height and piston skirt set the timing. Changing a port height changes the open period and the compression ratio. For this reason, port timing is used in tuning small motorcycles, chainsaws and outboard motors; see Unit 4 for scavenging details.

figure.caption: The timeline runs in crank degrees. The current-cycle inlet and exhaust bars show the open periods; the 20° overlap is the common opening around TDC, from 10° before TDC to 10° after TDC.

spec.aria: A crank-angle timeline shows the inlet valve open from 10 degrees before TDC to 40 degrees after BDC, the exhaust valve open from 45 degrees before BDC to 10 degrees after TDC, and the 20-degree valve overlap around TDC.

examples.question: A four-stroke SI engine has the inlet valve opening 10° before TDC and closing 40° after BDC. The exhaust valve opens 45° before BDC and closes 10° after TDC. Find the inlet open period, the exhaust open period and the valve overlap in crank degrees.
steps: Draw the 720° cycle. TDC at start of intake = 0°. BDC after intake = 180°. Use the inlet lead 10° and inlet lag 40°.
Exhaust opens 45° before BDC and closes 10° after TDC. Exhaust open period = 45° + 180° + 10° = 235°CA.
Overlap is the common open time around TDC: inlet lead + exhaust lag = 10° + 10° = 20°CA. Count it once.
examples.answer: Inlet open period = 230°CA, exhaust open period = 235°CA, valve overlap = 20°CA.
examples.check:
lead_in = 10
lag_in = 40
lead_ex = 45
lag_ex = 10
inlet_period = lead_in + 180 + lag_in
exhaust_period = lead_ex + 180 + lag_ex
overlap = lead_in + lag_ex
print(inlet_period)
print(exhaust_period)
print(overlap)

traps: Crank degrees, not cam degrees: in a four-stroke the cam turns 360° while the crank turns 720°. A 20°CA overlap is 10° of cam rotation.
Do not add overlap twice: it is the common open period around TDC, already inside the inlet and exhaust periods if you compute from lead and lag.
Before and after both add: inlet lead is before TDC and inlet lag is after BDC, so the inlet period is lead + 180° + lag.
Valve timing is not ignition timing: spark or injection near the end of compression is a separate event; do not mark it as valve overlap.
A simple two-stroke port diagram is symmetric about BDC for exhaust and transfer; do not copy the asymmetric cam lead and lag values into it.

quiz.a: Valve overlap is the crank-angle period near TDC when both inlet and exhaust valves are open together.

quiz.q: Why does the exhaust valve open before BDC?
quiz.a: To use cylinder pressure for blowdown, start removing burnt gas, and reduce pumping work on the exhaust stroke.

quiz.q: An engine has inlet opens 12° before TDC, closes 50° after BDC; exhaust opens 40° before BDC, closes 15° after TDC. Find the inlet period, exhaust period and overlap.
Why is SI valve overlap kept small at idle but can be larger at high speed?
quiz.a: At idle, low inlet pressure and high exhaust pressure can reverse flow through the open valves; at high speed, gas inertia is stronger and more overlap improves breathing.

quiz.q: In a simple two-stroke port timing diagram, which port opens first near BDC?
quiz.a: The exhaust port opens first; the transfer port opens later.

quiz.q: Compare a valve timing diagram with a port timing diagram in one sentence.
quiz.a: A valve timing diagram shows cam-controlled valve events in a four-stroke; a port timing diagram shows piston-controlled port events in a two-stroke.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines now use variable valve timing and cam phasers to change lead, lag and overlap with speed and load. Miller and Atkinson cycles use early or late inlet closure to change the effective compression ratio. Two-stroke port design is studied with scavenging models and CFD. Search for variable valve timing, cam phaser, Miller cycle and port timing diagram.
